_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 4 Inputs Decide Outputs. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order: one question two answers, inputs decide outputs, writing a branch, building a loop, checking it. Which branch a frame lights is never decided by the film: the lesson's own ART.algo.branchRun is run on the lesson's own round data, and the picture draws what it returns. The unrolled count comes from ART.algo.expandLoop for the same reason.
title: Inputs Decide Outputs
subtitle: Grade 4 Computing
objectives: Know how to develop algorithms to produce different outputs based on different inputs.
Know how to develop algorithms that include repetition.
Predict the outcome of algorithms that contain repetition.

beats.say: Is it raining? Yes, take an umbrella. No, take sunglasses.
One question, two answers, and the input decides which steps run.
An algorithm can fork. It asks one question about its input.
Leaving for school: get dressed, pick up your bag. Then the question.
Is it raining? Yes: put on your raincoat and take the umbrella.

at.steps: your raincoat and take the umbrella

beats.say: No: put on sunglasses and take a sun hat. Then walk to school.

at.steps: sunglasses and take a sun hat

beats.say: The steps before and after are the same. Only one answer's steps run.

at.same: before and after are the same

beats.say: Change the input, and the same algorithm gives a different output.
Raining in. The yes steps run, and out come the raincoat and the umbrella.
Sunny in. The no steps run, and out come the sunglasses and the sun hat.

at.out: the sunglasses and the sun hat

beats.say: A quiz program is the same. A right answer in: a tick, a point and well done.

at.out: a tick, a point and well done

beats.say: A wrong answer in: a cross and a hint. The input decided both times.
To write a branch, first choose the question that decides it.
Borrowing a book. The question is: is the book on the shelf?

at.ask: is the book on the shelf?

beats.say: You look on the shelf whatever the answer, so that step goes first.
On the shelf: take it to the desk and scan your card.

at.steps: take it to the desk and scan your card

beats.say: Not there: ask for it to be saved. Thanking the librarian happens either way.

at.steps: ask for it to be saved

beats.say: Now test it both ways. A step in the wrong place turns up for one answer only.
Water three plants. The same three steps happen for every plant.
Fill the can, pour on a plant, walk to the next. Those go in the loop.
Set the count to three, and the loop does those steps three times.
You get the can out of the shed once, so it stays outside the loop.

at.can: get the can out of the shed

beats.say: Putting the can away happens once too, after the loop has finished.
To check a loop, unroll it. Write out every step it really does.
Three steps, three times round, makes nine steps.
The can is fetched once before and put away once after. Eleven in all.
Does it do the whole job and nothing extra? Then the loop is right.
Four plants instead? Change the count to four. Nothing else moves.
A branch is a fork: one question, and a rule for each answer.
Different inputs take different branches, so you get different outputs.
Steps that repeat go in a loop, and the count says how many times.
